title: Back Pain: Causes, Self-Care, and When to Seek Help
content:
Back pain is one of the most common reasons people seek medical care and a leading cause of work absence worldwide. Most acute back pain (lasting less than 4–6 weeks) resolves with self-care and does not indicate serious disease.

Common causes of non-specific low back pain include muscle or ligament strain from sudden movement or poor lifting technique, prolonged sitting or standing, poor posture, and deconditioning of the core and back muscles. These are mechanical causes — they are not dangerous and typically improve with movement rather than rest.

Self-care for acute non-specific low back pain:

Continue moving. Bed rest is no longer recommended for most back pain — it can actually slow recovery. Gentle walking and light activity within the limits of comfort help maintain flexibility and reduce muscle spasm.

OTC pain relief: ibuprofen (an NSAID that also reduces inflammation) or paracetamol (acetaminophen) taken according to package instructions can manage pain enough to allow movement. Apply ice in the first 48 hours (15–20 minutes at a time, with a cloth barrier) to reduce inflammation; heat may help after the first day or two for muscle relaxation.

Position relief: lying on your back with a pillow under your knees, or on your side with a pillow between your knees, can reduce strain on the lower back.

Return to normal activities as quickly as comfort allows — this speeds recovery.

Seek medical attention promptly (same day or emergency) for back pain with any of the following "red flag" symptoms, which may indicate a serious underlying cause: loss of bladder or bowel control (possible spinal cord compression — a medical emergency); numbness or weakness in both legs; pain following a significant trauma (fall, accident); pain accompanied by fever, unexplained weight loss, or history of cancer; pain that is severe, constant, worsens at night, or is not relieved by any position.

Chronic back pain (lasting longer than 12 weeks) benefits from a comprehensive approach including physiotherapy, exercise, and in some cases pain management input. Surgery is rarely indicated and should be considered only after conservative treatment has been tried.
source: Original — based on NIH NIAMS back pain guidance and NHS back pain self-care information (public domain summaries)
